Qualified clock dependency — accepted user decision, 2026-10-10

Authority: the user selected "Allow the qualified clock dependency (recommended)"
in response to the clock question on 2026-10-10. The separately accepted
all-owner-loss decision is recorded below.

The first profile may condition its physical UTC deadline on a named, qualified
clock dependency remaining within a stated error bound. It must test its response
to reported faults. It need not promise detection of every silent clock error.
If that dependency silently exceeds its bound, the physical deadline can be
missed; detection must retain the failure evidence, not report the bound as met.

This decision approves no numeric skew, horizon or enforcement allowance. It does
not qualify a source or establish the missing Fargate evidence semantics. T-01
must still establish a coherent current UTC interval, source/sample relationship,
freshness, timescale, validity/holdover and conservative local deadline binding.
Reported faults and uncertainty require the selected fail-closed response; unknown
required properties reject before sensitive input release.

Keep the original absolute expiry fixed. Restart, resume or new time evidence must
not renew work authority. Keep uncertain execution, scratch and capacity fenced.
Admit no new execution before independently verified termination and required
cleanup. All other isolation, resource, result, recovery, clock/reboot and hosted
evidence requirements remain. T-01 remains incomplete.

All-owner-loss limit — separately accepted user decision, 2026-10-10

Authority: the user selected "Allow this all-owner-loss limit (recommended)" on
2026-10-10. The question asked whether T-01 may exclude simultaneous loss of every
trusted cleanup owner from the physical deletion deadline, while preserving a
surviving owner for required controller, broker and single-runner failures.

The first profile may exclude simultaneous loss of every trusted cleanup owner
from its physical deletion deadline. Required controller, broker and single-runner
failures still require a surviving owner and proof of the selected bounded cleanup
path. If all owners die, deletion may be late. Record a missed physical bound;
quarantine is not deletion. Keep the original expiry fixed and admit no new
execution before independently verified termination and required cleanup.

This exclusion does not excuse payload-induced loss of all owners through
inadequate isolation or resource protection; that remains a design failure.
The exact owners, authority, resource protection, disposal path and fault evidence
remain to be established. No cleanup mechanism or numeric allowance is adopted.

Both decisions are accepted; neither remains pending. They grant no new implementation, deployment or merge authority. All other requirements and existing holds remain.

Select the first protected profile and simplest feasible execution approach, with reproducible containment/recovery evidence and two materially different deployment models under D-07.

Use disposable synthetic inputs and bounded disposable resources. Stop/fence discovered invocations and retain unresolved evidence; do not broaden host privileges or weaken the profile to make the spike pass. ## Decisions and design
D-01 — Accepted planning direction: general managed processor invocations.
The contract owns execution of registered native workloads with bounded opaque inputs and results. Payload schemas, domain interpretation, intake/storage workflows and business authorization belong to downstream applications. Feasibility fixtures exercise execution requirements and do not define library-specific content types or domain processors.
The application supplies an authorized bounded input and interprets the result. Runledger owns registration, durable admission/identity, execution, deadline enforcement, result fencing, settlement and recovery. An adapter owns concrete execution/transport; deployment owns provisioning and enforcing external identity/network/storage configuration. Processors receive no database, key-store or orchestration authority. A trusted broker or native worker is distinct from the untrusted payload processor. A separate Runledger-specific remote service is optional.

D-02 — Accepted: one concrete, fail-closed initial profile; defer a general profile language.
T-01 must define the initial profile before evaluating mechanisms. Assume a fully compromised registered native executable. Name protected secrets, other inputs, broker/worker authority and host resources; allowed channels/files/egress; input/output, CPU, memory, process-count, scratch and duration bounds; and the exact controller/broker/host failure assumptions. Select only the confidentiality/disposal properties required for this first profile. Bind a registered processor/revision to that validated contract, with fresh per-invocation containment; reuse of compromised native processor state is deferred. Required unsupported or unknown properties reject before sensitive input release. An explicit unresolved outcome preserves failure evidence; it never counts as satisfying a requested hard resource or lifetime bound. Distinguish memory-only from encrypted ephemeral scratch, cooperative cancellation from executor-side lifetime enforcement, and process supervision from isolation. Deployment assumptions and evidence have provenance; a Rust witness is not proof of remote configuration. The application chooses a declared profile; adapters cannot weaken it. Processor executable/entrypoint and permitted options are fixed by trusted registration. Untrusted input/result fields cannot select commands, images, mounts, host paths or arbitrary fetch URLs; artifact descriptors are scoped capabilities, not unchecked path/URL strings.

D-03 — Accepted: library-owned phase order.
A canonical processor-job registration supplies trusted preparation and application callbacks around runtime-owned admission -> durable intent -> authorized input transfer -> execution -> candidate-result handoff -> required execution/scratch settlement -> fenced application and native completion -> candidate-result disposal. Preparation may reject without launching; authorize/audit immediately before plaintext transfer, and revalidate authority after any capacity/startup wait. Avoid holding plaintext while awaiting unbounded admission. Work factories are inert before polling/admission. T-01 selects one initial input/result-transfer approach: bounded native streams or explicitly scoped immutable artifact access. Do not build both without a demonstrated need, or persist raw bytes, reusable grants or presigned URLs as queue metadata.
Keep generic contracts free of storage/provider dependencies. Extend native persistence/runtime; keep mechanism-specific SDKs and tooling optional. The Batter adapter only integrates native startup/shutdown and reexports justified native APIs.

D-04 — Accepted: durable invocation identity and independent evidence.
Persist a stable execution identity linked to job/run/attempt, immutable input identity, processor/profile revision, backend binding, absolute durable expiry and bounded sanitized observations before launch. Never serialize a local Instant. Work budgets cannot grow on restart or through transport delay. Specify a trusted time source and conservative conversion to local monotonic clocks, an explicit tolerated skew bound and fail-closed behavior when expiry cannot be established. Name the trusted component that independently arms/enforces expiry and the allowed enforcement delay for each supported failure domain. Prove controller/broker loss while the processor environment remains alive; killing their shared host/container proves a different property. Cover restart/reboot, suspend/resume and clock rollback within the stated fault model. Settlement has its own bounded observation allowance without extending work authority.

The first profile may condition its physical cleanup deadline on stated maximum host scheduling, notification and I/O delays. This is an additional dependency beyond the accepted full-host-freeze limit. A platform delay beyond those limits can make physical deletion late and must be recorded as a missed bound. Quarantine is not physical deletion.

Payload-caused starvation remains a design failure. The accepted dependency does not excuse inadequate isolation, exhausted recovery resources or an unbounded cleanup algorithm. State independently meaningful host-service limits and bounded workload/operation counts; derive the cleanup allowance from them. Use native durable reservations associated with invocations, reconciled independently of the current job lease. Uncertain launches and possibly live executions remain accounted across retry, cancellation, dead-lettering, reaping and worker death. Define protected no-overlap over a stable native invocation lineage for one logical processor job/workflow step, preserved by direct replay and workflow recovery even when new job/run IDs are allocated. No replacement execution in that lineage while the previous one remains unresolved. Workflow active-key/resource release must consider outstanding processor invocations, not only live canceled leases. New unrelated roots are not globally deduplicated by content hash; applications use explicit resource/idempotency policy when they require cross-root exclusion. Bound outstanding unknown executions and admission waiters across replicas; do not add a general quota engine. Compute, sensitive scratch and retained candidate-result obligations may settle at different times and require separately bounded accounting. Retention/purge cannot cascade away unresolved records, reservations or late-launch tombstones.
Strict no-overlap is an explicit conservative first-release policy: it avoids introducing an overlapping-replay contract while preserving existing workflow resource/exclusion expectations. It can block a lineage indefinitely under uncertainty; T-01 must establish whether that availability cost and containment procedure are acceptable. Side-effect-free duplicates can be valid under another contract with complete aggregate accounting and fenced acceptance; they are not inherently a security defect, but are not enabled here. Workflow coverage is retained; omitting it requires explicit rejection of unsupported processor workflow compositions and a scope amendment.
Use the existing native recovery machinery. A remote runner may use native invocation persistence or its selected executor's durable inventory, but must not grow a second job queue, workflow engine or fleet manager. Recovery control is trusted; the untrusted processor has only the exact input/result channel. Reserve bounded control/reconciliation resources so saturated execution admission cannot prevent recovery. T-01 rehearses full-capacity loss of observability and identifies the responsible operator, real execution-domain identity, supported containment action and evidence permitting reuse. If that evidence is unavailable, expose quarantined/unavailable capacity; deleting rows or operator approval alone is not settlement evidence.
Retries require explicit replay policy, established prior-execution eligibility and finite attempt/elapsed limits. Adapter observations determine infrastructure failures; processor bytes cannot invent them. Indeterminate and deterministic resource-limit failures cannot open an unlimited alternative retry budget.

D-06 — Accepted: untrusted results and fenced application effects.
Bound and validate transport envelopes and output; bind them to invocation, input and processor/profile revision. Require authenticated encryption with peer/endpoint verification for every remote control, input and result hop; authentication alone is insufficient. Any buffered sensitive artifacts obey the selected confidentiality/retention profile. Authenticate narrowly scoped grants; consider replay, wrong audience, expiry, wrong-attempt results and metadata-service/ambient-credential access. Define the authorization linearization point and any online redemption/revocation check or bounded remaining validity of offline grants. Revocation does not recall delivered bytes or necessarily interrupt an already authorized stream.
T-01/T-02 must choose and encode candidate-result handoff semantics. Either retain a bounded recoverable result (or immutable reference) until durable acknowledgement/acceptance permits disposal, or explicitly allow loss and apply finite replay/reauthorization policy only after prior execution is settled. Identify the last recoverable copy and owner at each transfer, including controller death after delivery but before apply, domain rejection, acknowledgement loss and application-commit uncertainty. Processor scratch disposal and candidate-result disposal are different obligations. Apply/retention recovery must reconcile exact acceptance before garbage collection; exceeding retention cannot silently discard an unresolved required copy or create unbounded result storage.
Provide an owned native transaction scope that rechecks current run/attempt/execution authority after locking, then calls application SQL and records application acceptance, native job/attempt completion, events and workflow consequences in the same transaction. There is no acknowledged application commit followed by a separate success write. Expose reusable in-transaction native transitions through the existing owned SQLx foundation; do not call the current independently committing public success entrypoint from the callback or add a parallel transaction abstraction. Current domain authority is application-owned and checked in that same transaction. Duplicate applications must be idempotent or rejected; lost commit acknowledgement is reconciled from that exact invocation/acceptance identity before replay. The runtime must not repeat application SQL after reconciling an identified committed acceptance; the callback can run again after a confirmed rolled-back attempt under explicit retry policy. No owned connection/transaction or separately paired commit token is supplied on the canonical path. PgScopedSql exposes a query executor for trusted SQL; it cannot prevent explicit transaction-control SQL, direct manipulation of ledger tables, or effects through independently captured clients. Those are excluded escapes, not supported compositions or evidence of rollback when detected. T-02 must record this upstream/application trust boundary under ADR-010, demonstrate the explicit-COMMIT negative control, and name any minimal shared SQLx seam needed; do not build a SQL sandbox or weaken ordinary library-owned completion. Runledger performs no non-database execution/transport I/O while holding the application transaction. Arbitrary async callbacks can perform external I/O; those effects remain application-owned and outside the atomicity guarantee. Isolation and result authentication do not establish application-level result correctness, malware absence or arbitrary remote rollback.
Diagnostics use bounded codes and redacted reports; raw input/output/stderr are not automatic logs or durable results.

D-07 — Accepted: evidence-led deployment selection without a mandatory provider or remote service.
T-01 compares (a) an existing trusted Runledger worker next to established local isolation, with the producer elsewhere, (b) an optional binding to an established managed execution service, and (c) a narrow authenticated remote runner where trust/deployment requirements justify it. Provider-specific SDKs may live in optional adapters; the core and application contract remain provider-independent. Moving a worker changes which host holds application/database authority; document that tradeoff rather than treating it as equivalent to a credential-isolated remote broker.
Select two materially different supported deployment models and only the bindings they require. They may share an isolation primitive or adapter; two identical hosts or an RPC wrapper around a local handle do not establish diversity. T-05 implements the selected first binding; T-06 proves the second model and implements another binding/remote protocol only if needed. T-01 updates their concrete scope and reuse edge before downstream execution. A custom runner is limited to bounded start/observe/stop/recover and inventory; no business queue, workflow/retry policy, host placement or fleet lifecycle.
For each candidate, map controller/worker, broker if any, processor, ledger/inventory and sensitive artifact placement, privileges/credentials, enforcement owner and recovery operator. Separately state application portability, executor deployability and operational prerequisites. The evaluation must address a restricted managed-container deployment model without privileged orchestration in the application container, and disclose any independently operated privileged service elsewhere. T-01 names the actual target deployment test required before claiming that operational problem solved; T-08 records its evidence. Local restriction emulation can support only the exercised claims, not substitute for a hosted result. Cloud provisioning needs separate authorization; missing access leaves that target unverified, not falsely complete.
Generic runtime APIs contain no Docker/Kubernetes/cloud resource specification. Native SQLx/PostgreSQL 18 remains authoritative. A warm trusted broker may be reused with fresh processor containment. Additional profiles, warm native-processor reuse, a new weaker supervised mode, extra backend families, generic artifact frameworks and nonessential operator UI are deferred. No universal shell runner, plugin marketplace, antivirus service, application policy engine or arbitrary user-code hosting platform.

## Primary references
Checked during architecture review on 2026-09-26; recheck exact selected upstream releases in T-01 and record them in docs/references.md during implementation.
- TLS 1.3: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446#section-1 — confidentiality, integrity and peer authentication are separate transport requirements.
- Docker security: https://docs.docker.com/engine/security/ — daemon authority and runtime isolation depend on configuration.
- Kubernetes Pods: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/ — containers in one Pod share networking; grouping alone is not the declared boundary.
- Kubernetes Jobs: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/job/#handling-pod-and-container-failures — parallelism=1 and restartPolicy=Never can still produce duplicate starts; physical execution and replacement semantics need verification. Rechecked 2026-09-26.
- Managed timeout example: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/batch/latest/userguide/job_timeouts.html — best-effort timeout termination and per-attempt countdowns are not an independently proven total lifetime bound. Rechecked 2026-09-26.
- Kubernetes RuntimeClass: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/containers/runtime-class/ — backend selection is a deployment mechanism.
- AWS Fargate security: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/fargate-security-considerations.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/fargate-tasks-services.html — task boundaries and unsupported Docker-style controls illustrate why profiles cannot be flag translations.
- Wasmtime security/interruption: https://docs.wasmtime.dev/security.html and https://docs.wasmtime.dev/examples-interrupting-wasm.html — optional capability-based mechanisms; no native-workload compatibility claim.

## Alternatives
Ordinary subprocess + env_clear supplies useful supervision, not the protected isolation boundary. A mandatory container-per-job/cloud-task application API fixes one deployment shape. A provider-neutral trait that leaves lifecycle coordination to applications retains the original problem. Optional bindings to established platforms are live T-01 alternatives under D-07. Building a new sandbox or general orchestration service exceeds this epic.
